explanation: Fires mostly on digits or separators in the middle of long identifier strings, such as citation keys ([@pone.0062400], [@B2-micromachines-10-00324]) and date/ID path segments in URLs (2015/08, 18139261). It fires most strongly on scientific-article citation IDs. Scattered moderate activations on ordinary words in academic prose do not share any clear pattern.

Fires on a word-initial subword token, most strongly a capital or lowercase 'M'/'m' that starts a word split into pieces (m|auling, M|AGA, M|uppets, M|mmm, M|ateria), especially names and non-English words. It fires more weakly on other word-starting fragments like 'pl', 'sol' and '-V'. Whole common words do not activate it.

Fires on tokens inside SEO-style web page titles and headings, i.e. keyword-stuffed noun phrases at the start of a commercial/product/service page (e.g. 'TrailBlazer Ratings, Reviews [and] Analysis', 'Tire Service ... [near] Lynchburg', 'SATA DRIVER [DOWNLOAD]'). It fires strongest on the connective or keyword token in the middle of such a title. Ordinary running prose gives weak or no activation.

A diffuse mix with no single theme. It fires on leading digits of dates, years and reference numbers (May [1]9, 2006-08-[0]2, @bib[0]020) and also on common function words like 'the' and 'a' in ordinary prose, plus scattered code tokens. Its response to a new token is hard to predict.

Fires on tokens inside geopolitical text about nations, ethnic groups, regions and political bodies, especially in names or descriptions of non-Western states and peoples (Arab states, Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, Slavic Wagrians, Pakistan Peoples Party, Africa's most populous). The marked token is usually a nationality or political-entity word, or a word in a phrase about one. Text with no geopolitical content stays weak.

A mixture of unrelated jobs. It fires on tokens in boilerplate code and markup (Bootstrap class names like 'col-lg-' and 'row-fluid', 'UTF-8', the word 'License' in software license headers, 'will' in the GPL phrase 'in the hope that it will be useful'), on 'embry'/'stem'/'immortal' in stem-cell biology text, and on one forum 'Originally Posted'.

Fires on the determiner or quantifier right after 'for' in 'for X reason' idioms: 'for [a] reason', 'for [whatever] reason', 'for [some] reason', 'For [this] reason', 'for no [particular] reason'. It fires more weakly on other words that introduce a cause or explanation ('partly explained', 'can't understand why'). Without a reason/cause context it is near zero.

Fires on tokens in code and math notation where an argument, assignment or set/range is being given. Examples are Python call keywords and method names ('args=', '.append', '.reshape', 'for i in'), '=' and opening brackets in LaTeX set or tuple definitions, and the word 'range' in 'within the range [a,b]'. Plain prose does not activate it.

Fires on a comma that ends a noun phrase naming a topic or entity, just before an elaboration or appositive. Its strongest case is the patent opener 'The present invention relates to X[,] and more particularly...'. It also fires on commas before appositives and 'such as' or 'including' lists. Commas between clauses in casual prose get weak to moderate activation.

Fires on the word-initial subword 'pl'/'Pl' (and 'pla', 'ple', 'plan') that starts a word broken into pieces, in any language: Plakat, Plasma, plombée, Plasmodium, platted, plenty, plenary. Other word-initial fragments ('Poly', 'Air') get only weak activation.

Fires on the final subword piece of a rare or foreign proper noun or non-English word: name endings ('Cakob[au]', 'Chay[ka]', 'Pettine[o]'), species epithets ('geoffren[sis]'), place-name endings ('Albertsl[und]', 'Köpen[ick]') and foreign word suffixes. Common English words do not activate it.
